claims.text: Rapid quenching can produce a metastable amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
The as-quenched amorphous alloys contain internal stresses and structural heterogeneities that promote early crystallization.
A sub-Tg anneal applied after quenching will improve glass-forming ability.
A sub-Tg anneal applied after quenching will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Heating an amorphous alloy can cause changes in its short- and medium-range atomic configurations.
A sub-Tg hold allows the amorphous structure to access a lower-energy glass configuration.
A properly selected sub-Tg hold remains below the activation threshold for crystallization.
Sub-Tg structural relaxation reduces internal stress.
Sub-Tg structural relaxation decreases the density of potential crystallization sites.
The anneal produces more uniform atomic packing and fewer defects.
The proposed relaxation mechanism raises the crystallization onset temperature during subsequent heating.
Annealed samples will show a statistically significant increase in DSC-measured crystallization onset temperature relative to as-quenched controls.
The post-quench anneal may increase shear modulus or hardness relative to as-quenched controls.
The intervention is beneficial only when the as-quenched alloy is fully amorphous and the annealing temperature lies narrowly below Tg.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration can cause premature crystallization.
Applying the anneal promptly after quenching is necessary for the expected benefit.
A brief hold on the order of minutes under an inert or controlled atmosphere is an appropriate process window.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims improved glass-forming ability, but the intervention is applied only after the glass has already formed. The predicted outcomes and experiment measure post-formation crystallization stability and mechanical properties, not glass-forming ability under a controlled cooling or casting condition.
